title: 1934 United Airlines Utah crash
summary: A Boeing 247 departing Salt Lake City in severe winter weather crashed nose-first into Parley's Canyon at high speed. The aircraft was flying in clouds and fog through mountainous terrain with no visual references and hit the mountain with such force that the nose was thrust deep into the earth.
probable_cause: The cause was not immediately determined but poor weather and terrain collision were contributing factors; investigators acknowledged they might never determine the exact cause due to the extent of damage.

factors.evidence: The weather was poor, with snow and sleet throughout the region, with up to 7 in of snow accumulating in the lowlands.
The aircraft flew in clouds and fog; weather was called 'the worst in the history of flying in this region.'
Departure was at 14:00 and officials said fuel would be exhausted by 06:30, indicating flight in darkness.
The aircraft was flying through clouds and fog in mountainous terrain without visual references.
Aircraft was found nose-down in Parley's Canyon, having apparently flown straight into the ground at high speed.
The aircraft crashed nose-first into the mountain with the nose thrust into the earth; every part except wings was smashed.

events.text: Boeing 247 NC13357 departed Salt Lake City bound for Cheyenne with severe weather including snow and sleet throughout the region
Last radio word from aircraft was pilot Lloyd Anderson signaling 'All Okay' 20 minutes after departure

title: 1934 Air France Wibault 282T crash
summary: On 9 May 1934, an Air France Wibault 282T departed Le Bourget for Croydon carrying three crew and three passengers. The aircraft passed over Le Tréport at 12:10 and received a radio position fix at 12:19 over the English Channel. With low cloud cover across the route, the aircraft disappeared without an SOS distress call, crashing into the sea while attempting to descend below cloud base. All six occupants were killed.
probable_cause: The aircraft crashed into the English Channel while attempting to fly below low cloud base without adequate visual reference, likely incapacitating the crew before a distress call could be sent.

factors.evidence: At the time, the weather conditions included low cloud cover
The absence of an SOS call from the aircraft indicated that it had crashed into the sea while attempting to fly below the low cloud base
The aircraft crashed into the English Channel off Dungeness

title: 1934 Swissair Tuttlingen accident
summary: Swissair Condor II CH-170 cruising at 3,000 meters encountered a thunderstorm shortly after crossing the Swiss-German border. The right wing experienced structural failure from oscillation-induced stress fractures, exacerbated by violent turbulence. The wing separated from the fuselage and the aircraft fell into a forest near Tuttlingen, exploding on impact. All 12 occupants, including Europe's first air stewardess Nelly Diener, were killed.
probable_cause: Structural failure of right wing resulting from stress fractures caused by wing oscillations and engine vibrations, which were exacerbated by violent thunderstorm turbulence and defective welding techniques in construction.

factors.evidence: Aircraft encountered thunderstorm with violent turbulence while cruising at 3,000 metres
Oscillations in the wing caused stress fracture, severity exacerbated by violent weather conditions
One fracture formed in wing and engine-mount structure due to defective construction and welding techniques in conjunction with engine vibrations
Right wing broke off; plane fell into forest near Tuttlingen, exploding into flames on impact

Right wing broke off aircraft; plane fell into forest near Tuttlingen and exploded on impact

title: 1934 London, Scottish & Provincial Airways Airspeed Courier crash
summary: An Airspeed Courier on a scheduled flight from London to Paris encountered a thunderstorm over northwest Kent. The aircraft emerged from clouds in a vertical dive at a cloudbase of 1200 ft with hills reaching 600 ft. The pilot, an experienced RAF veteran with 1500 hours, may have stalled attempting to avoid high-tension power lines. The aircraft crashed north of Shoreham with all four on board killed.
probable_cause: An eyewitness suggested the pilot may have stalled trying to avoid power lines after encountering storm conditions.

factors.evidence: An eyewitness stated that he thought the pilot may have stalled trying to avoid high tension power lines.
The aircraft flew into an isolated storm over north west Kent.
The aircraft emerged from the clouds in a vertical dive at a cloudbase of 1200 ft with hills around Shoreham reaching 600 ft elevation.
The aircraft crashed just north of Shoreham in Timberden Bottom, at the bottom of Cockerhurst Road.

title: 1934 Hillman's Airways de Havilland Dragon Rapide crash
summary: A de Havilland DH.89A Dragon Rapide operated by Hillman's Airways crashed into the English Channel off Folkestone on October 2, 1934, killing all seven occupants. The aircraft departed Abridge at 10 am in marginal visibility with 700 feet cloudbase and 2 miles visibility which deteriorated in rain. The pilot requested a radio bearing from Croydon which indicated the aircraft was north of Dover; the pilot turned south to correct course. At 11:02, with visibility poor in patchy rain and 300 feet cloudbase, the aircraft dived into the sea 4 miles off Folkestone. An Air Ministry investigation determined the cause was pilot error due to lack of experience in navigation and blind flying, with poor visibility preventing visual reference to the sea surface.
probable_cause: Pilot error due to lack of navigation and blind flying experience; pilot unable to distinguish sea surface in poor visibility conditions and descended into the water.

factors.evidence: Visibility decreased to 2 miles initially and deteriorated further to poor in patchy rain with 700 feet cloudbase reducing to 300 feet.
Pilot received radio bearing from Croydon placing him north of Dover and turned south to regain course; aircraft position not accurately determined.

Aircraft dived into English Channel 4 miles off Folkestone at 11:02, was destroyed and all seven occupants killed.

title: 1934 KLM Douglas DC-2 crash
summary: KLM Douglas DC-2 Uiver crashed during a publicity flight from Cairo to Baghdad in a rainstorm and burst into flames near Rutbah Wells, killing all seven crew and passengers. The investigation revealed KLM had taken excessive risks, ignored multiple important safety aspects, and the aircraft had incomplete maintenance adjustments. The Dutch Minister issued airworthiness certificate with fewer demands than required. Poor weather conditions combined with inadequate aircraft preparation contributed to the accident.
probable_cause: Poor weather conditions during flight combined with inadequate aircraft preparation. Investigation found KLM responsible for taking excessive risks and ignoring safety aspects, with regulatory oversight failure in certificate approval.

factors.evidence: The aircraft crashed during a rainstorm; very bad weather occurred at the time of flight though this forecast was unknown when the airplane left Cairo
